findings.detail: The capital programme is heavily weighted to a £106.62m Sustainable Communities for Learning scheme across four schools (2026-27 to 2027-28). The strategy states the Council will borrow approximately £16.20m for new school projects. Separately, the risk section identifies that 'costs potentially exceeding available budgets' from construction inflation, supply chain difficulties, and wage pressures. The document warns that schemes 'may need to be reprioritised based on the available funding' if procurement reveals higher costs.
findings.matters: Large committed schemes with multi-year delivery risk combined with real cost inflation creates material exposure to budget slippage or scheme deferral, affecting both capital programme completion and revenue servicing assumptions.
findings.figures: £121.82m total 2026-27 expenditure; £106.62m for Sustainable Communities for Learning (four schools) 2026-27 to 2027-28; £16.20m new borrowing for schools; £19.37m Porthcawl Grand Pavilion 2026-27 to 2027-28.
findings.quote: The Council will need to borrow approximately £16.20 million in order to fund new school projects in line with the Council's Schools Modernisation Programme.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising as proportion of revenue budget, with explicit concern about future borrowing capacity
findings.detail: Table 10 shows capital financing costs (net) rising from 1.97% of revenue in 2025-26 to 2.06% by 2029-30. The strategy explicitly states: 'An increasing ratio limits the scope for additional borrowing in future years and reduces the Council's overall flexibility when making decisions on the allocation of its revenue resources.' The document further warns: 'it will be increasingly difficult to secure revenue funding to meet the costs of any new borrowing.'
findings.matters: Rising financing costs constrain future flexibility and signal mounting debt service pressure relative to available revenue, which is material for credit assessment and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Capital financing costs: 1.97% (2025-26) rising to 2.06% (2029-30). CFR forecast increase of £16.31m in 2026-27.
findings.quote: An increasing ratio limits the scope for additional borrowing in future years and reduces the Council's overall flexibility when making decisions on the allocation of its revenue resources.

findings.headline: Welsh Government capital funding increase is modest and insufficient for identified pressures
findings.detail: Welsh Government's capital allocation increased from £4.772 million to £4.992 million for 2026-27 (a £220,000 increase) and is described as modest. This increase is set against multiple cost pressures that could outpace funding growth.
findings.matters: Funding growth that lags inflation and identified cost pressures signals the Council will face tighter capital constraints and may need to borrow or defer schemes.
findings.figures: £4.772 million to £4.992 million; future estimates remain at increased level
findings.quote: Welsh Government's capital funding allocation to the Council for 2026-27 shows a slight increase to that previously anticipated, from £4.772 million to £4.992 million, and future estimates show funding as remaining at this increased level. It is a modest increase

findings.headline: Capital receipts are largely committed, constraining new scheme funding
findings.detail: The Council's capital receipts are heavily allocated to existing schemes within the capital programme. This limits the Council's ability to fund new capital schemes without additional borrowing. The Council notes that funding new schemes is challenging and may require securing specific grants and other external funding.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether a council has flexibility to fund capital investment or whether it must borrow for incremental needs, which adds to debt service costs.
findings.figures: Capital receipts largely committed to existing schemes; Welsh Government funding at £4.992 million for 2026-27
findings.quote: with the Council's capital receipts largely committed to schemes within the capital programme, funding any new schemes is challenging

findings.headline: Dependency on SEWCJC accounts which have had recurring quality and timing delays
findings.detail: The council consolidates transactions and balances from the South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee. The auditor noted 'delays in certification...due to the late submission...and longer than anticipated audit periods due to the quality of those draft accounts'. For 2025-26, 'SEWCJC accounts production remains a risk for the preparation of the Council's financial statements particularly with the certification deadline coming forward to the end of September 2026'.
findings.matters: A council's consolidated accounts depend on timely, high-quality information from partner bodies. When partners have demonstrated quality issues, it creates risk that the council's own reporting will be delayed or contain errors.
findings.figures: SEWCJC is material enough to consolidate into the council's Statement of Accounts, affecting CIES, Balance Sheet and MIRS
findings.quote: The delay in certification has been due to the late submission of the SEWCJC draft accounts and longer than anticipated audit periods due to the quality of those draft accounts and complexity of transactions contained within them. Looking forward to next year, the timeliness of the SEWCJC accounts production remains a risk for the preparation of the Council's financial statements for 2025-26 particularly with the certification deadline coming forward to the end of September 2026.

findings.headline: Audit deadline acceleration to September 2026 is at risk due to current working paper quality and complexity dependencies
findings.detail: The auditor explicitly warned that working paper preparation timeliness is a 'potential issue in achieving the deadlines for future years' when the audit window compresses further. The council currently struggles to have all working papers ready at audit start, and depends on the South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee (SEWCJC) for consolidated figures, which itself has had quality and timeliness issues.
findings.matters: Audit deadline failures create uncertainty in financial reporting timelines and can flag governance or operational capacity issues; missing deadlines puts pressure on the council's ability to report accurately.
findings.figures: Deadline moving to 31 October 2025 for 2024-25; further acceleration to 30 September 2026 for 2025-26
findings.quote: We are conscious that when the accounts production and audit window reduce next year, this could be a potential issue in achieving the deadlines for future years.

findings.headline: Repeated errors in asset valuation spreadsheets despite three years of audit recommendations
findings.detail: The auditor noted errors in property revaluation spreadsheets for the third consecutive year. Although described as 'trivial' and totalling £252k understatement, the report states 'This year we again identified errors within the revaluation spreadsheets as a result of incorrect formulas'. The council has been implementing a new asset management system to address this, but the pattern of recurrence suggests control weaknesses in the current process.
findings.matters: Repeated control failures on asset valuations—even if individually immaterial—indicate systemic weaknesses in financial controls and suggest risk of undetected errors in other areas.
findings.figures: £252,000 total understatement from spreadsheet formula errors; £1.517 million and £2.369 million corrections to asset valuations
findings.quote: In 2022-23 and 2023-24, we reported issues arising from our audit of property, plant and equipment... This year we again we identified errors within the revaluation spreadsheets as a result of incorrect formulas used (as opposed to errors in the revaluations themselves as set out in Appendix 2). These were trivial and amounted to understatements of £252k in total.

findings.headline: Borrowing figures required significant audit corrections and working papers had clarity issues
findings.detail: The auditor identified that working papers for borrowings were 'not clear and concise and required revision after submission' and there were 'significant delays in responding to audit queries in these areas'. A £2.389m understatement of non-current borrowing was corrected by management. Given that borrowing is material to a council's financial position, the combination of working paper quality issues and large corrections suggests controls around borrowing accounting need attention.
findings.matters: A lender depends on accurate, clearly-documented borrowing figures. Weak working papers and significant post-audit corrections indicate control or documentation weaknesses that could mask other issues.
findings.figures: £2.389 million understatement of non-current borrowing corrected; £8.712 million carrying amount and £8.764 million fair value of short-term financial liabilities incorrectly excluded from disclosure
findings.quote: Two areas of particular concern were borrowings and cash where the working papers were not clear and concise and required revision after submission to us. There were also significant delays in responding to audit queries in these areas, which extended the time required for the audit.

news_drafts.headline: Interest rate outlook highly uncertain due to Iran-Israel conflict; forecaster predicts upside risk to Bank Rate with potential hikes in coming months
news_drafts.lead: Rate rises would materially worsen debt service costs across the £99.72m borrowing portfolio; timing is acute given the July LOBO refinancing and forecast 2026-27 borrowing of £30.37m would be taken at potentially higher rates.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Outturn Report 25-26

news_drafts.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to rise £21.21m year-on-year to £203.77m (2026-27), driven by capital programme commitments
news_drafts.lead: Rising CFR indicates expanding capital commitments funded by debt; limits debt capacity and signals extended period of elevated borrowing requirements, increasing refinancing and interest rate risk.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Outturn Report 25-26

news_drafts.headline: Liability benchmark forecasts £30.37 million additional borrowing requirement in 2026-27, up sharply from £55.45m at year-end
news_drafts.lead: Represents a material increase in external financing need for the coming year; combined with maturing debt (£7.79m PWLB + £0.40m Salix in 2026-27) and the July LOBO refinancing, creates substantial near-term borrowing demand.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Outturn Report 25-26
